questions.question: An annual unit life annuity-due has a three-year guarantee and pays at integer times from issue. Which payment dates are guaranteed irrespective of survival?
options: Times 1, 2 and 3.
Times 0, 1, 2 and 3.
Times 0, 1 and 2.
Time 0 only; times 1 and 2 require survival.

questions.question: A five-year guaranteed annual life annuity-due pays one unit at times 0 through 4 irrespective of survival. The annuitant dies at time 1.5, and a designated beneficiary receives outstanding guaranteed instalments. Which description matches the stated contract?
options: The beneficiary receives no further instalments after time 1.5.
The beneficiary receives units at every later annual date without limit.
The beneficiary automatically receives three units together at time 1.5.
The beneficiary receives the scheduled units at times 2, 3 and 4.

questions.question: A life annuity-due has a four-year guarantee at dates 0 through 3, followed by annual payments only while the annuitant lives. The annuitant is alive at time 7. What happens to the payment at time 7?
options: It is not paid because the four-year guarantee has expired.
It is paid to the annuitant because they are alive.
It is paid to the beneficiary even though the annuitant is alive.
It is paid irrespective of whether the annuitant is alive.

questions.question: A unit annual annuity-due has integer guarantee $n\ge 1$. Let $T>0$ be non-integer future lifetime and $K=\lfloor T\rfloor$. Which formula gives the total payment count, including beneficiary receipts, for every admissible $n,T$?
options: $\max(n,K)$

questions.question: A three-year guaranteed annuity-due pays 100 annually at times 0, 1 and 2, then only while the annuitant survives. The discount factor is $v=0.9$ and death occurs at time 0.5. What is the realised total PV, including beneficiary receipts?

A unit annuity-due has a four-year guarantee, annual discount factor $v=0.8$, and probability 0.7 that the annuitant survives to time 4. Assume no atom at the payment date. What is the APV contribution of the payment at time 4 alone?

An annual unit annuity-due is extended from a three-year to a four-year guarantee, with all other terms unchanged. The annual discount factor is $v=0.9$ and $P(T>3)=0.8$, where $T$ is future lifetime; there is no death atom at 3. How much does its APV increase?

A unit guaranteed annuity-due has certain-prefix PV $C$ and deferred survivor-tail PV $R$, so total PV is $G=C+R$. The tail can take at least two values with positive probability. What uncertainty remains in the total value?
options: The total is certain because the first payments are guaranteed.
Only the guaranteed prefix is random.
The total varies only when the annuitant dies during the guarantee.
The total remains random through the survivor tail.

questions.question: Compare a unit annual annuity-due with an integer guarantee period n>=1 to its otherwise identical ordinary life annuity-due. Payments and discount factors are non-negative and APVs are finite. Which APV comparison holds for every admissible guarantee period and mortality law?
options: The guaranteed APV is strictly greater on every mortality basis.
The guaranteed APV is at least the ordinary APV.
The guaranteed APV is at most the ordinary APV.
The APVs are equal because surviving lives receive the same stream.

questions.question: A unit annual annuity-due has a three-year guarantee. Its certain-prefix PV is 2.71, $v=0.9$, survival probability to time 3 is 0.6, and the unit ordinary annuity-due APV conditional on survival to 3, valued at 3, is 9. What is its total issue APV?

A unit annual annuity-due has a three-year guarantee and annual discount factor $v=1/2$. The annuitant future lifetime is otherwise unspecified. Which interval uses the greatest universal lower bound and least universal upper bound as its endpoints?

A unit annual annuity-due has a two-year guarantee and discount factor $v=1/2$. With probability 0.3, future lifetime $T$ is uniform on $(0.1,0.9)$ years; otherwise it is uniform on $(3.1,3.9)$ years. Which is the distribution of its total PV?
options: Value $1$ with probability 0.3; value $1.875$ with probability 0.7.
Value $1.5$ with probability 0.7; value $1.875$ with probability 0.3.
Value $1.5$ with probability 0.3; value $1.75$ with probability 0.7.
Value $1.5$ with probability 0.3; value $1.875$ with probability 0.7.

questions.question: An ordinary unit annual life annuity-due is revised by guaranteeing its first four dates $0,1,2,3$. Let $T>0$ be absolutely continuous future lifetime, $0<v<1$, and both APVs be finite. Which mortality condition is necessary and sufficient for the revised APV to be strictly higher?

Two unit annual annuities-due have a three-year guarantee and discount factor $v=0.8$. Under model A, future lifetime is uniform on $(3.1,3.3)$ years. Under model B, with equal probabilities it is uniform on $(1.1,1.3)$ or on $(5.1,5.3)$ years. Their mean lifetimes both equal 3.2 years. Which APV comparison is correct?
options: The APVs agree at $2.952$ because the mean lifetimes agree.
Model B gives $2.74464$, below model A value $2.952$.
Model B gives $3.68928$, above model A value $2.952$.
Model B gives $3.06464$, above model A value $2.952$.

questions.question: A unit annual annuity-due has a four-year guarantee, positive discount factor $v=0.9$ and finite APV. Its observed APV equals exactly the certain-prefix value $1+v+v^2+v^3$. Let $T$ be continuous future lifetime. What must follow about survival to time 4?
options: $P(T>4)$ can be positive if later survivor receipts offset earlier deaths.
$P(T>4)$ is determined only by the interest rate.
